Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $n\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous, let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be order-convex with at least two elements, and let $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous with $t_0\in I$ and $(t,x(t))\in D$. A curve solves the IVP if and only if it satisfies the associated Volterra integral equation. Explicitly, the equation is

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

derivations.claim: Write each component as a finite sum $F_i(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}c_{i\alpha}x^\alpha$. On any bounded coordinate box, for each exponent $q\ge1$ the identity $a^q-b^q=(a-b)\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}a^{q-1-j}b^j$ bounds the difference of each monomial at two points by a finite constant times their Euclidean distance; telescoping over the $N$ factors and summing the finitely many monomials proves that $F$ is locally Lipschitz there. It is also continuous, so [F1] applies at every state.

Put $R_+=\max(1,R)$ and $M_R=\bigl(\sum_{i=1}^N(\sum_{\alpha\in E_i}|c_{i\alpha}|R_+^{|\alpha|})^2\bigr)^{1/2}$. Since $|x_j(t)|\le R$ for each coordinate, the finite polynomial sums give $\|F(x(t))\|_2\le M_R$ for all $t<T_*$.

For $0\le s<t<T_*$, apply [F3] to $x|_{[s,t]}$ to obtain $\|x(t)-x(s)\|_2\le M_R(t-s)$. Hence $x(t)$ is Cauchy as $t\uparrow T_*$; for example, the sequence $t_n=T_*(1-1/n)$ for $n\ge2$ is Cauchy after applying this bound. By [F2] it converges to some $x_*\in\mathbb R^N$. For any $t<T_*$ and all sufficiently large $n$ with $t_n\ge t$, the same bound gives $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(t_n-t)+\|x(t_n)-x_*\|_2$; letting $n\to\infty$ yields $\|x(t)-x_*\|_2\le M_R(T_*-t)$, so $x(t)\to x_*$. The closed-ball bound passes to the limit, hence $\|x_*\|_2\le R$.
By step 1.1 the polynomial field is locally Lipschitz near $x_*$. Apply [F1] to the IVP at $(T_*,x_*)$ to obtain a local solution $y$ on an open interval about $T_*$.

By [F4], $x(t)=x_0+\int_0^tF(x(s))\,ds$ for $t<T_*$ and $y(t)=x_*+\int_{T_*}^tF(y(s))\,ds$ near $T_*$. The limit in step 3.1 and continuity of $F$ extend the first identity to $t=T_*$. Define $\widetilde x=x$ before $T_*$ and $\widetilde x=y$ from $T_*$ onward, assigning the common value $x_*$ at $T_*$. The joined curve is continuous and the two integral identities add to its Volterra equation on $[0,T_*+\epsilon)$ for some $\epsilon>0$; [F4] therefore makes it a $C^1$ solution of the same ODE extending $x$.
The extension in step 5.1 agrees with the original curve at every $t<T_*$ and is defined beyond $T_*$. This proves the statement.

Let $N\ge1$, let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be a polynomial map, and let $T_*>0$. Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

For each $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, the PDE is the finite-dimensional ODE $\dot{\widehat z}=-i\rho_* k\cdot\widehat v$, $\dot{\widehat v}=-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\widehat z$. For $k\ne0$, differentiating the first equation and substituting the second gives $\ddot{\widehat z}+c_*^2|k|^2\widehat z=0$. With $\omega_k=c_*|k|$, its unique solution is $\widehat z(t,k)=\widehat z_0(k)\cos(\omega_kt)-i\rho_*(k\cdot\widehat v_0(k))\sin(\omega_kt)/\omega_k$, and integrating the second mode equation gives $\widehat v(t,k)=\widehat v_0(k)-i(c_*^2/\rho_*)k\int_0^t\widehat z(s,k)\,ds$. Fix lengths $L_1,L_2>0$ and width $h>0$. Define the periodic channel
$$\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}=(\mathbb R/L_1\mathbb Z)\times(0,h)\times(\mathbb R/L_2\mathbb Z)$$
and the infinite channel
$$\Omega_{\infty}=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R.$$
Both have the product Euclidean metric. On $\Omega_{\mathrm{per}}$, the first and third coordinates are periodic quotient coordinates with periods $L_1$ and $L_2$; differential operators are the ordinary coordinate operators applied to periodic lifts. On $\Omega_{\infty}$, all three coordinates are ordinary real coordinates. The closures add the two wall faces at $y=0$ and $y=h$, and no other spatial boundary is imposed. A vector field is $C^\infty$ up to these walls when it is smooth in the interior and every spatial derivative of every order extends continuously to both faces on each compact coordinate patch. Its homogeneous no-slip boundary condition is $u=0$ on the two wall faces; prescribed wall velocity $g$ means the trace condition $u=g$. The definition imposes no decay or other condition at infinity on $\Omega_{\infty}$; such conditions must be stated separately.
